subject_line: Two Nicholas Royles and the hides in between
email_body:
Dear Nicholas,

An English Guide to Birdwatching turns the long confusion between two writers called Nicholas Royle into part of the novel's machinery, with the short 'Hides' pieces interrupting the story. Since then you have also written Mother, a memoir. I would be curious to hear how it felt to move from a book that plays so openly with names and identity to one where the self on the page is unmistakably your own, and what carried over between them.

subject_line: Michael, a golf ball, and imagining things away
email_body:
Dear Daniel,

In Nothing, Michael is knocked into a coma by a golf ball and wakes with no memory of his life, but convinced he can imagine things out of existence. The Big Issue's description of it as both a dark domestic drama and very funny suggests how finely balanced it is. I would like to ask where Michael's strange power came from, and how the next novel, Now and in England, is taking shape.

subject_line: Checking into Hôtel Amour after Erato
email_body:
Dear Deryn,

Hôtel Amour opens with a woman checking into a Paris hotel that is both real and imagined, and it picks up where Erato left off, returning to memory, desire and the body. I was struck that you chose to write a sequel to a poetry collection at all. I would like to ask what made you go back to that territory, and why a hotel, a place people pass through rather than settle in, became the right room for it.

subject_line: Mummers on the streets of The Alexandra Sequence
email_body:
Dear John,

The Alexandra Sequence looks at contemporary urban life through the mummers' play, the seasonal folk theatre once performed in the streets and from door to door, and takes its title from a Liverpool district. It is an unexpected lens for a city poem. I would like to ask how the mummers first entered the book, and whether the questions you raised in Poetry and Privacy about poetry's life outside academic and literary circles shaped that choice.

email_body:
Dear Adrian,

Bruise follows an injured fighter returning to his coastal hometown, which puts a body that has been trained to take damage back among the people who knew him before any of it. I would like to ask how you approached writing the fights themselves against the quieter scenes at home, and how teaching the workshop, the subject of your recent Bloomsbury book on the creative writing workshop in the twenty-first century, fed into finishing a debut novel.

subject_line: Britain in 1952, from Cold Crash to A Little Switch
email_body:
Dear Jennifer,

Your trilogy of historical thrillers, from Cold Crash, which won the Cinnamon Press debut novel prize, through The Running Lie to A Little Switch, stays within a narrow window of Britain in 1952 and 1953. That is a very deliberate frame: the war only just over, rationing still in force, a new reign beginning. I would like to ask why those two years drew you, and what it was like to live inside them across three books.

subject_line: From a field in Lahore to Orford Ness
email_body:
Dear Noreen,

A Flat Place begins with your earliest memory, a wide flat field seen from the back of your father's car in Lahore, and then travels through Britain's flatlands from Orford Ness to Orkney. I noticed that the UK edition is subtitled simply 'a memoir', while the US edition names empty landscapes and complex trauma outright. I would like to ask how you felt about those two framings, and which of the flat places stayed with you longest once the book was done.

subject_line: Eels, moths, mussels and crickets in Late Light
email_body:
Dear Michael,

Late Light follows four creatures most people overlook, eels, moths, freshwater pearl mussels and crickets, and it ties their decline to political apathy and economic pressure while insisting it is not an elegy. I was struck by that refusal of mourning as the default tone. I would like to ask how you chose those four, whether any of them surprised you once you started spending time with them, and what writing against elegy asked of you on the page.

subject_line: Bicycles in short supply at a Cape Cod Wendy's
email_body:
Dear Billy,

The title story of The Cape Cod Bicycle War puts immigrant workers at a Wendy's in wintry Cape Cod into competition over too few bicycles, while elsewhere in the collection a young man befriends an ageing gorilla at a Nairobi zoo. The East African read the book as a social history of millennial Kenya, yet several stories are set beyond it. I would like to ask how you think about that distance, and what you are writing now.

subject_line: Darcy, a wounded grizzly and a Yellowstone cabin
email_body:
Dear Mimi,

In Dreaming the Bear, Darcy is recovering from illness in her parents' Yellowstone cabin, mostly alone among the pines, when she comes face to face with a wounded grizzly and the two form a bond that edges into the dreamlike. Readers often single out that hazy, half-awake quality of the writing. I would like to ask how you balanced a real, dangerous animal against that dream logic, and what you now pass on to students on the Bristol MA about writing wild places.

subject_line: Birdy Arbuthnot saying yes in sixties Soho
email_body:
Dear Joanna,

Birdy Arbuthnot's Year of 'Yes!' sets a coming-of-age story in 1960s Soho, and the Carnegie shadowing notes describe it as told with grounded grace, which seems a nice counterweight to a decade usually written as pure noise and colour. You also write The Worst Class in the World for much younger readers. I would like to ask what drew you to Soho in that period, and how you move between the comic chaos of one series and a teenage novel like Birdy's.

subject_line: Beth Crowe and the poet who wrote Roslyn
email_body:
Dear Eimear,

In Holding Her Breath, Beth Crowe arrives at university in Dublin after a breakdown has ended her swimming career, and finds herself in the shadow of a grandfather whose final collection, Roslyn, was declared his masterwork after his death. I liked how the novel sets an athlete's discipline against a literary legacy she never chose. I would like to ask how you built the poet she never met, and whether co-founding Banshee changed the way you see literary reputations being made.

book_title: Wanderers: A History of Women Walking
subject_line: From Elizabeth Carter to Nan Shepherd on foot
email_body:
Dear Kerri,

Wanderers traces ten women writers who walked, across three centuries, from Elizabeth Carter to Nan Shepherd and Cheryl Strayed, and your work editing Shepherd's letters seems to carry that thread further. One reader complained the women in it never wander aimlessly, which struck me as the point: their walking was deliberate. I would like to ask how you chose those ten, who you were sorry to leave out, and which walk of your own you think about most.

subject_line: Elegies for Simic and Sweeney in After Party
email_body:
Dear Dean,

After Party carries elegies for Charles Simic and Matthew Sweeney alongside poems that start from ordinary rooms and strange premises, which feels like a fitting pairing, given how both poets made the uncanny feel domestic. It follows Kitchens at Night, your pamphlet from Smith Doorstop. I would like to ask what you owe to those two poets, how the kitchens of the pamphlet grew into a full collection, and how your year as UCC's Writer in Residence is going.

email_body:
Dear Paula,

A History of Running Away braids three women together: a boxer in 1980s Ireland, a gynaecologist in Dublin, and a young woman in Maryland. Joseph O'Connor singled out its vivid sense of place and person. I noticed it was first announced under a different title, A Difficult History, and I would like to ask what changed in the book between those two names, and why boxing sits at its centre.

book_title: Noon in Paris, Eight in Chicago
subject_line: Algren and de Beauvoir across six time zones
email_body:
Dear Douglas,

Noon in Paris, Eight in Chicago follows the on-off affair between Nelson Algren and Simone de Beauvoir, and The Skinny praised the documentary precision you brought to it. As a Chicagoan who has lived in England and Berlin since 1999, you seem well placed to write a love story split between two cities and two languages. I would like to ask whether your own distance from Chicago shaped how you wrote Algren, and what drew you next to Tin Pan Alley in the Sing for Life novellas.
